sections.html: Baltimore is an independent city, separate from any county since 1851, so city agencies handle jobs a county would handle elsewhere, from tax collection to land records. The population was 585,708 in 2020, down from a 1950 peak of 949,708. Rowhouses are the dominant house type, many with brick or formstone fronts, and the city is split into nine regions that match police districts. Popular rowhouse neighborhoods include Federal Hill, Fells Point, Canton, Hampden and Roland Park.

sections.h2: How Baltimore real property tax is billed
sections.html:
Bills go out every July 1. The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state rate of $0.112 per $100 appears on the same bill.

  • Bills are due on receipt, with a one-half percent discount if you pay by July 31.
  • Interest and penalties begin after October 1.
  • Late payments accrue 1 percent interest plus a 1 percent penalty per month.
  • Owner-occupied homes can pay in two equal parts, with the second due before January 1 and a small added fee.
  • An appeal does not excuse a late payment, but a successful one brings a refund with interest.

The Homestead Tax Credit caps yearly growth in taxable value for owner-occupied homes at 4%. The state sets assessments. In the January 1, 2026 reassessment, residential values in Baltimore City rose 13.4% over 2023, phased in over three years.

Baltimore holds its tax sale every May. A house can become eligible when a non-owner-occupied property owes $250 or an owner-occupied one owes $750.

WhenWhat happens
Early FebruaryFinal bill and legal notice mailed
MarchList of eligible properties published in two newspapers
First week of AprilSecond notice, covering amounts through April 30
April 30Last day to pay to avoid the sale
Third week of MayAnnual tax sale, normally
Six months after saleBuyer may sue to foreclose redemption on non-owner-occupied homes
Nine months after saleSame right for owner-occupied homes

The city cannot waive the fees and costs that state law sets for the bidder. A Tax Sale Deferral Program protects a property for one year without erasing the debt.

If you have fallen behind, you have two clean exits. Pay the balance by April 30 and the house comes off the sale list. Or sell to a buyer who clears the lien at settlement, so the unpaid tax is taken out of your proceeds and the title passes free of it.

The second route works best when you start well before the sale date. The notices in February, March and April are your warning signs. Once the May sale happens, the clock on the buyer's right to foreclose starts, and your choices narrow fast. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which helps when a deadline is close, but the lien still has to be paid before the deed is recorded.

As of January 28, 2022, Baltimore had 15,032 vacant houses, about 13,560 of them privately owned. The number came out when the mayor ordered a 30-day review of how city agencies handle vacants, after a fire and collapse at a vacant house killed three firefighters.

The city housing department files receivership cases against neglected vacants and was on track to file nearly 500 in that fiscal year. If you own a vacant or inherited house, selling before a case is filed keeps the property out of that process. Open code notices and liens still have to be settled at closing, so pull them before you list.

The city transfer tax is 1.5% of the consideration, and the state transfer tax adds 0.5%, for a total of 2%. The recordation tax is $5 for each $500 of consideration.

Transfers are processed in person at the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, Room 1B, 200 N. Holliday Street. Document processing is open to the public on Mondays and Wednesdays only. Each turn takes up to three documents, and each deed can cover up to three properties.

sections.h2: What to bring to record the deed
sections.html:
• A lien certificate, an original signed and notarized deed, an intake sheet, a copy of the settlement sheet and the contract of sale.
  • Proof that open liens are paid in full. Pay them before you sign in.
  • Separate checks payable to the Director of Finance for city transfer tax, recordation tax and any yield tax.

Simplifile is available if your closing agent prefers e-recording, which saves the trip downtown.

sections.h2: What a Baltimore seller must disclose
sections.html:
A seller of a house with four or fewer units must give the buyer a state disclosure or disclaimer statement on or before the day the contract is signed (Maryland Real Property Code 10-702). The disclaimer says the property is sold as-is, except for known latent defects.

Sales by lenders after foreclosure, sheriff and tax sales, and fiduciary transfers from estates and trusts are exempt. If the buyer is not given the form on time, the buyer can rescind within five days after receiving it. Hand it over early and keep a signed copy.

sections.h2: Can I sell a vacant Baltimore house as-is?
sections.html:
Yes. Maryland allows an as-is sale with a disclaimer statement, and cash buyers often prefer houses that need work. The sale does not erase anything attached to the property. Liens, tax debt and open code notices are paid or settled at closing, so a title search early in the process tells you what the final number will look like.

Gather the tax bills, any city notices and the deed before you talk to buyers. Offers move faster when the paperwork is ready, and you avoid surprises at the settlement table.

faqs.q: What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, plus a $0.112 state rate on the same bill.

faqs.q: When are Baltimore property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed July 1 and due on receipt. Interest and penalties start after October 1, and a one-half percent discount applies if you pay by July 31.

faqs.q: What is the Baltimore transfer tax?
faqs.a: The city transfer tax is 1.5% and the state transfer tax is 0.5%, a total of 2% of the consideration. Recordation tax is $5 per $500.

faqs.q: When does the Baltimore tax sale happen?
faqs.a: It is normally held in the third week of May. April 30 is the last day to pay and avoid the sale. Non-owner-occupied homes become eligible at $250 owed and owner-occupied homes at $750.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Baltimore?
faqs.a: At the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, 200 N. Holliday Street, Room 1B, on Mondays and Wednesdays, or through e-recording with Simplifile. Bring the lien certificate and the notarized original deed.
